notes.definition: Waves transfer energy (and information) from one place to another without transferring matter. In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
explanation: A wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium (or through a vacuum, for electromagnetic waves). As the wave passes, the particles of the medium oscillate (vibrate) about a fixed position, but they do not travel along with the wave. What moves from place to place is energy. This is why waves are so useful for communication: they can carry energy and information over large distances while the medium stays where it is.

In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction in which the wave transfers energy. If you flick a rope tied to a wall, each part of the rope moves up and down while the wave travels horizontally along it. Ripples on the surface of water are transverse, and so are all electromagnetic waves such as light, radio waves and X-rays. Transverse waves have peaks (crests) and troughs.

In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Pushing and pulling one end of a stretched slinky spring produces a longitudinal wave. The coils bunch up in some places, called compressions, and spread out in others, called rarefactions. Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal: the air particles vibrate backwards and forwards along the direction the sound travels, creating regions of higher and lower pressure.

There is clear evidence that it is the wave, not the water or air, that travels. If a cork or a small floating object is placed on water in a ripple tank or a pond, it bobs up and down as ripples pass but does not move across the water with them. Similarly, when someone speaks to you, the air near their mouth does not travel to your ear; only the sound energy does. A ribbon tied to a slinky moves back and forth but stays in the same place on average.

Longitudinal waves need a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel through, because they work by particles pushing on neighbouring particles. That is why sound cannot travel through a vacuum such as space. Mechanical transverse waves, such as ripples or waves on a string, also need a medium, but electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that can travel through a vacuum.
keyFacts: Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter.
Particles in the medium oscillate about a fixed position; they do not travel with the wave.
Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
Examples of transverse waves: ripples on water, waves on a string, all electromagnetic waves.
Examples of longitudinal waves: sound waves in air, a slinky pushed and pulled along its length.
Longitudinal waves have compressions (particles close together) and rarefactions (particles spread out).
A floating cork bobs up and down but does not move along with a water ripple.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles to vibrate.

keyTerms.definition: A disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
A repeated back and forth (or up and down) movement about a fixed position.
A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are closest together (higher pressure).
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are furthest apart (lower pressure).
The substance (solid, liquid or gas) that a wave travels through.

workedExamples.title: Classifying a wave from its motion
workedExamples.question: A student holds one end of a long slinky on a bench and moves her hand quickly left and right across the bench, at right angles to the slinky. Is the wave transverse or longitudinal? Explain how you know.
steps: Identify the direction of energy transfer: along the length of the slinky.
Identify the direction of oscillation: left and right across the bench, at right angles to the slinky.
Oscillation perpendicular to energy transfer means the wave is transverse.
workedExamples.answer: Transverse, because the coils oscillate at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction in which the wave transfers energy.

workedExamples.title: Using evidence that the medium does not travel
workedExamples.question: A leaf floats on a pond. A stone is dropped in and ripples spread out past the leaf. Describe what happens to the leaf and explain what this shows.
steps: As each ripple passes, the leaf rises and falls.
After the ripples have passed, the leaf is in (almost) the same place as before.
If the water travelled with the wave, the leaf would be carried to the edge of the pond.
So the water oscillates up and down, but only the energy of the wave moves outwards.
workedExamples.answer: The leaf bobs up and down but stays in the same place. This shows that the wave transfers energy across the pond, not the water itself.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the water in a ripple or the air in a sound wave travels along with the wave.
misconceptions.right: In fact the particles only oscillate about a fixed position. The wave transfers energy, not matter.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sound is a transverse wave because it is drawn as a wavy line on an oscilloscope.
misconceptions.right: In fact sound in air is longitudinal. The oscilloscope trace is a graph of how the pressure (or microphone signal) changes with time, not a picture of the wave's shape.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'longitudinal' means the wave is long and 'transverse' means it goes across a short distance.
misconceptions.right: In fact the names describe the direction of oscillation compared with the direction of energy transfer: parallel for longitudinal, perpendicular for transverse.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all waves need a medium.
misconceptions.right: In fact electromagnetic waves such as light can travel through a vacuum. Sound and other mechanical waves need a medium.

realWorld: Sound travels to your ears as a longitudinal wave: your eardrum is pushed and pulled by compressions and rarefactions in the air.
Surfers ride the energy of ocean waves; the water mostly moves in circles rather than travelling to the beach with the wave.
Mobile phones and Wi-Fi use transverse electromagnetic waves to carry information through the air and through space without any material being sent.
examTips: When defining transverse and longitudinal waves, always compare the direction of oscillation with the direction of energy transfer. Saying 'the wave goes up and down' is not enough for the mark.
Use the words 'perpendicular' and 'parallel' (or 'at right angles' and 'in the same direction as'). Avoid 'the wave moves sideways'.
Learn one example of each type: ripples on water (transverse) and sound in air (longitudinal). EM waves are also transverse.
If asked for evidence that the wave and not the medium travels, describe a floating object (cork) bobbing up and down on ripples, or explain that air does not travel from a speaker to your ear.
On a diagram of a longitudinal wave, label compressions where the lines are closest together and rarefactions where they are furthest apart.
summary: Waves transfer energy and information, not matter.
Particles oscillate about a fixed position as a wave passes.
Transverse waves: oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer (ripples, EM waves).
Longitudinal waves: oscillations parallel to energy transfer (sound).
Longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions.
A cork on ripples bobs up and down but is not carried along.

questions.question: What do all waves transfer from one place to another?
options: Matter
Particles of the medium
Energy
Mass and energy
markScheme: 1 mark: Energy
questions.explanation: Waves transfer energy (and information) but not matter. The particles of the medium oscillate and stay, on average, in the same place.

questions.question: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
options: A sound wave in air
A ripple on a pond
A light wave
A radio wave
markScheme: 1 mark: A sound wave in air
questions.explanation: Sound waves in air are longitudinal. Ripples on water are transverse, and light and radio waves are electromagnetic waves, which are all transverse.

questions.question: How do the oscillations in a transverse wave compare with the direction of energy transfer?
options: They are parallel to it
They are in the opposite direction to it
They are in random directions
They are perpendicular to it
markScheme: 1 mark: They are perpendicular to it
questions.explanation: Transverse means the oscillations are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of energy transfer. Parallel oscillations describe a longitudinal wave.

markScheme: 1 mark: A longitudinal wave is produced with compressions and rarefactions
questions.explanation: Moving the end along the length of the slinky makes the coils oscillate parallel to the energy transfer, so a longitudinal wave with compressions and rarefactions travels along it. The coils oscillate about fixed positions and do not travel to the end.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a small piece of cork floating on the water in a ripple tank.
Ripples travel from left to right.
What happens to the cork as the ripples pass?
options: It moves up and down but stays in about the same place
It is carried to the right with the ripples
It moves left and right in the same direction as the ripples
It stays completely still
markScheme: 1 mark: It moves up and down but stays in about the same place
questions.explanation: Ripples are transverse, so the water (and cork) oscillates up and down, perpendicular to the energy transfer. The cork is not carried along because the water does not travel with the wave.

questions.question: Why can sound waves not travel through a vacuum?
options: A vacuum absorbs all sound energy
Sound waves are transverse and need a surface
There are no particles to vibrate and pass on the wave
Sound travels too fast to be detected in a vacuum
markScheme: 1 mark: There are no particles to vibrate and pass on the wave
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave. It is passed on by particles colliding with neighbouring particles. In a vacuum there are no particles, so sound cannot travel.

questions.question:
A sound wave travels through air.
Which statement about an air particle in the path of the wave is correct?
options: It travels from the source to the listener at the speed of sound
It vibrates at right angles to the direction of travel
It moves steadily away from the source and does not return
It vibrates back and forth along the direction of travel, with no overall movement
markScheme: 1 mark: It vibrates back and forth along the direction of travel, with no overall movement
questions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave each particle oscillates parallel to the direction of energy transfer about a fixed position. It does not travel to the listener; only the energy does.

questions.question: Which observation is the best evidence that it is the sound wave, and not the air, that travels from a loudspeaker to a listener?
options: The sound gets quieter further from the speaker
The sound can be heard through a closed door
A candle flame in front of the speaker flickers back and forth but does not get blown steadily away
The sound reaches the listener almost instantly
markScheme: 1 mark: A candle flame in front of the speaker flickers back and forth but does not get blown steadily away
questions.explanation: The flame moving back and forth shows the air oscillating about a fixed position. If air flowed from the speaker, the flame would be pushed steadily away. The other observations are true but do not show that the air does not travel.

questions.question: Name the quantity that is transferred by all waves.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy (allow information)
questions.explanation: Waves transfer energy and can carry information. They do not transfer matter.

questions.question: Give one example of a transverse wave and one example of a longitudinal wave.
markScheme: 1 mark: transverse example, e.g. ripples on water, light or any EM wave, wave on a string
1 mark: longitudinal example, e.g. sound wave in air
questions.explanation: Ripples and all EM waves are transverse. Sound waves are longitudinal.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
acceptedAnswers: transverse oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer
longitudinal oscillations parallel to direction of energy transfer
markScheme: 1 mark: in transverse waves the oscillations are perpendicular / at right angles to the direction of energy transfer
1 mark: in longitudinal waves the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer
questions.explanation: Both parts must compare the direction of oscillation with the direction of energy transfer (or wave travel).

markScheme: 1 mark: X is a compression, where particles are close together
1 mark: Y is a rarefaction, where particles are spread out / far apart
questions.explanation: Region X is where the lines (particles) are bunched together: a compression. Region Y is where they are spread out: a rarefaction. Compressions and rarefactions alternate along a longitudinal wave.

questions.question:
A duck is sitting on a pond.
Ripples pass the duck.
Explain why the duck is not carried to the bank by the ripples.
acceptedAnswers: water does not travel with the wave
markScheme: 1 mark: the water (and duck) oscillates up and down about a fixed position
1 mark: the wave transfers energy, not the water / matter
questions.explanation: As each ripple passes, the water rises and falls. The ripple moves outwards but the water stays where it is, so the duck is not carried along.

questions.question: What is the name given to the substance that a wave travels through?
markScheme: 1 mark: medium
questions.explanation: The substance through which a wave travels is called the medium, for example air for sound or water for ripples.

questions.question:
Light from the Sun reaches the Earth.
The sound of explosions on the Sun does not reach the Earth.
Explain this difference.
Refer to the types of wave in your answer.
acceptedAnswers: light is electromagnetic can travel through vacuum
markScheme: 1 mark: space is (almost) a vacuum
1 mark: sound is a longitudinal (mechanical) wave that needs particles / a medium to vibrate
1 mark: light is an electromagnetic (transverse) wave that can travel through a vacuum
questions.explanation: Sound is passed on by vibrating particles, so it cannot cross the vacuum of space. EM waves such as light do not need a medium.

questions.question:
A student makes this statement.
'In a sound wave, the air moves from the loudspeaker to your ear.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
acceptedAnswers: air particles vibrate about a fixed position
markScheme: 1 mark: air particles oscillate / vibrate backwards and forwards about a fixed position
1 mark: energy is transferred to the ear, not the air itself
questions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave the particles pass energy on to their neighbours by vibrating and colliding. They do not travel from source to listener.

questions.question: Name the type of wave that all electromagnetic waves are.
markScheme: 1 mark: transverse
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma, are transverse.

markScheme: Indicative content:
stretch slinky along a bench / floor, fix or hold far end
for transverse: move the end from side to side (perpendicular to the slinky)
coils oscillate at right angles to direction of energy transfer; peaks and troughs seen
for longitudinal: push and pull the end along the length of the slinky
coils oscillate parallel to direction of energy transfer; compressions and rarefactions seen
coils do not travel along the slinky; a tied ribbon stays in place on average
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of both waves including direction of coil movement relative to energy transfer.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes how to make one wave or gives simple statements about both without directions.
questions.explanation: A side to side movement gives a transverse wave; a push and pull along the length gives a longitudinal wave. In both cases the coils only oscillate and the energy moves along the slinky.

questions.question:
Compare transverse waves and longitudinal waves.
Your answer should include:
• how the particles move
• the features of each wave
• examples of each wave
• evidence that waves transfer energy but not matter.
markScheme: Indicative content:
both transfer energy (and information) without transferring matter
transverse: oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer
transverse features: peaks / crests and troughs
transverse examples: ripples on water, waves on a string, all EM waves (light)
longitudinal: oscillations parallel to direction of energy transfer
longitudinal features: compressions and rarefactions
longitudinal example: sound in air
sound needs a medium; EM transverse waves can cross a vacuum
evidence: cork on ripple tank bobs up and down but is not carried along
evidence: air does not travel from speaker to ear / ribbon on slinky stays in place
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, coherent comparison covering particle motion, features, examples and evidence.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes both types with some features or examples; evidence may be limited.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both waves, little comparison.
questions.explanation: A strong answer contrasts the direction of oscillation, names features (troughs/peaks versus compressions/rarefactions), gives examples, and uses the cork or slinky evidence to show that matter is not transferred.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a ripple on water?
options: Longitudinal; water oscillates parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Transverse; water oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
Transverse; water travels in the direction of energy transfer
Longitudinal; water oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
markScheme: 1 mark: Transverse; water oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
questions.explanation: Ripples are transverse: the water surface moves up and down while energy moves across the surface. The water is not carried along.

questions.question:
A wave in a solid makes the particles oscillate in the same direction as the wave travels.
Which feature would this wave have?
options: Regions of higher and lower pressure
Peaks and troughs on the surface
The ability to travel through a vacuum
Particles that travel along with the wave
markScheme: 1 mark: Regions of higher and lower pressure
questions.explanation: Oscillations parallel to travel mean the wave is longitudinal, so it has compressions (higher pressure) and rarefactions (lower pressure). Longitudinal waves cannot travel through a vacuum, and particles never travel with a wave.

questions.question:
A Mexican wave travels around a football stadium. Each spectator stands up and then sits down as the wave passes.
Suggest whether this is a model of a transverse wave or a longitudinal wave.
Give a reason for your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: transverse (people move up and down, perpendicular to the direction the wave travels around the stadium)
questions.explanation: Each spectator moves vertically while the wave travels horizontally around the stadium, so the movement is perpendicular: a model of a transverse wave. The spectators also stay in their seats, just as particles do not travel with a wave.

questions.question: Which word describes the movement of particles as a wave passes through a medium?
options: Flow
Evaporate
Oscillate
Diffuse
markScheme: 1 mark: Oscillate
questions.explanation: Particles oscillate (vibrate) about a fixed position as a wave passes. They do not flow along with the wave.
